Spit
SPIT
v.t. & v.i.
From Anglo-Saxon spittan, to eject saliva from the mouth. Webster 1828: to throw out saliva from the mouth. In Scripture the act is almost never merely physical; it is the body’s shorthand for contempt, and the law made it a formal sign of disgrace (Numbers 12:14; Deuteronomy 25:9).

Biblical Definition

Of all the indignities laid on the Lord Jesus, spitting is the one He named in advance and the one Isaiah saw seven centuries early. I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting (Isaiah 50:6). The Servant does not merely endure the insult; He declines to hide from it. Christ repeats the prophecy as a plain itinerary: they shall mock him, and shall scourge him, and shall spit upon him, and shall kill him: and the third day he shall rise again (Mark 10:34) — and the Sanhedrin fulfils it word for word: Then did they spit in his face, and buffeted him (Matthew 26:67). Understand what the face is in Hebrew thought. To seek God’s face is to seek His favour; to have Him hide His face is judgment. Men spat on the face of God incarnate. Yet the same Lord had used spittle as a means of mercy: he spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man (John 9:6). What man aimed at Him in contempt, He had already turned toward man in healing — the exchange the whole gospel runs on.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SPIT as to eject or throw out saliva from the mouth; and notes the biblical usage in which spitting on a person is the extreme public token of contempt and rejection.

SPIT, v.t. — To eject from the mouth; to throw out, as saliva.

SPIT, v.i. — To throw out saliva from the mouth.

To spit in or on the face, in the Scriptures, is a mark of the deepest contempt and abhorrence.

SPITTLE, n. — The moist matter of the mouth; saliva.

Anglo-Saxon spittan, spatl, saliva; connected with spew and sputter.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 50:6 — "I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting."

Mark 10:34 — "And they shall mock him, and shall scourge him, and shall spit upon him, and shall kill him: and the third day he shall rise again."

Matthew 26:67 — "Then did they spit in his face, and buffeted him; and others smote him with the palms of their hands,"

John 9:6 — "When he had thus spoken, he spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay,"

Modern Corruption

A sentimental modern piety keeps the cross solemn but scrubs it of squalor, and in doing so it loses the doctrine: it was shame, not only pain, that the Servant bore.

expand to see more

Preaching that dwells on the physical mechanics of crucifixion while passing quickly over the spitting has the emphasis backwards. Isaiah 53 puts contempt at the centre — despised and rejected of men — and the spitting is contempt made visible. The Reformed doctrine of Christ’s humiliation (the state of humiliation, running from the incarnation to the burial) holds that our Lord bore not only the penalty of sin but its disgrace. The 1689 Confession speaks of Him enduring most grievous torments in His soul and most painful sufferings in His body; the soul-torment is the harder half, and being spat upon by the creatures He made is a fair sample of it. Any account of the atonement that treats the cross as a transaction in pain alone has not reckoned with the face that men spat upon.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the exchange at the heart of the gospel. Christ received on His face what our sin deserved, and used spittle from that same mouth to open a blind man’s eyes. He was shamed that we might be honoured; He was rejected that we might be received. Numbers 12:14 shows the weight of the sign — if a father had but spit in his daughter’s face, she would bear the shame seven days. The Son bore the Father’s face turned away and men’s spittle upon His own, and did not hide.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew roq (H7536), spittle; yaraq (H3417), to spit; Greek emptuo (G1716), to spit upon; ptuo (G4429), to spit; ptusma (G4427), spittle.

expand to see more

Hebrew yaraq (H3417) — to spit; used of the formal disgrace in Deuteronomy 25:9 and Numbers 12:14.

Hebrew roq (H7536) — spittle; I hid not my face from shame and spitting (Isaiah 50:6).

Greek emptuo (G1716) — to spit upon, the compound of en (upon) and ptuo; used of the Passion in Matthew 26:67 and Mark 10:34.

Greek ptuo (G4429) — to spit; used of the Lord’s healing act in John 9:6.

Greek ptusma (G4427) — spittle, the noun behind the clay our Lord made in John 9:6.

Usage

"I hid not my face from shame and spitting (Isaiah 50:6) — the Servant does not merely endure the insult; He declines to hide from it."

"Then did they spit in his face (Matthew 26:67) — the face of God incarnate, and the face is where favour lives in Hebrew thought."

"He spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle (John 9:6) — what men aimed at Him in contempt, He had already turned toward man in healing."
